source_note: Robert C. Zuppke, Football Technique and Tactics, first edition, Copyright 1922, Zuppke and Bearg, Urbana, Illinois (title page PDF 7). Internet Archive scan with OCR text layer; full 184-page chunked read (17 near-empty pages are plates/endpapers, inspected). Page-1 retraction check: none — cover OCR noise only, no publisher notice. QUALITATIVE SOURCE: zero printed equations; all LaTeX is explicitly labeled predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rules. Printed page numbers run 14 behind PDF pages (PDF 15 = printed 1); citations use PDF pages. OCR artifacts preserved verbatim in quotes ('vards' for yards, hyphenated line breaks 'terri- tory', 'comple- tion', 'un- less', 'antici- pated'). Printed numbers used as printed historical data only: 1921 Big Ten game statistics (PDF 157-161), zone depths, 'forty vards' exchange ideal. No modern measurements invented; no sportsbook odds anywhere.

primitives.name: Play-cycle pre-snap indistinguishability (Zuppke play cycle completeness rule)
primitives.verbatim_quote: I am convinced that no group of plays is complete un- less each carries one or two straights, one or two slants, one angle and one or two forward passes, all starting from the same initial formation.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: C = play cycle set (one or two straights, one or two slants, one angle play, one or two forward passes from one initial formation; dimensionless set). Obs_pre = pre-snap observable state (formation, stances, mannerisms; information channel, dimensionless sigma-algebra). p,q = play indices (dimensionless). pi = prior probability measure over cycle members (probability units, sums to 1). Pr = posterior probability (probability units). No physical units: pure information/probability statement. Formalization of printed prose, no source equation.
primitives.assumptions: Predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rule; the source contains NO equations. Printed assumptions: all cycle members start from the same initial formation (p. 61 printed / PDF 75); later plays inherit mannerisms of earlier ones ('the third and fourth inheriting some of the mannerisms of the parent first and second', PDF 75); defense must not be informed before execution which of the second, fourth, or sixth play is coming (PDF 76). Assumes the defense's only pre-snap evidence is formation/stance/mannerisms and that drill can equalize them across plays. Printed-page offset: PDF page = printed page + 14.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when any play leaks a telltale initial movement ('quickly observing with the snap of the ball the telltale initial movements of the backs', PDF 76), when a back's stance or mannerism indicates style/direction during signals (PDF 62), or when the angle play's forward/backward decision is 'telegraphed' by looks or actions (PDF 75). Also fails if the cycle is overloaded: complexity breeds indecision and mistakes (PDF 70, 74). Indistinguishability is a drilled property, not a free one; it degrades under fatigue and under opponent film study that detects residual cues.
timescales: tau_0 = pre-snap orientation / signal cadence (order 1-5 s; modeling convention, not printed)
tau_1 = snap-to-first-contact (order 1-3 s; modeling convention)
tau_2 = whole-play execution (order 4-8 s; modeling convention)
tau_3 = drive/game/season learning and system drill (minutes to weeks; modeling convention)

layer2.mapping: Binds to the information channel between offense pre-snap state and defense posterior in the 22-player dynamical system: the play cycle is a constrained encoder that holds the pre-snap observation sigma-algebra constant across a mixture of run/pass actions, so the defense's transition-kernel selection (commit to line vs drop into coverage) must stay mixed until post-snap evidence resolves it. State variable: defense belief vector over play types; constraint: Obs_pre equality across cycle members; the angle play (PDF 75) is the run/pass branch point that keeps the posterior unresolved longest.
layer2.telemetry: Printed calibration: 1921 Big Ten game, 'A' 8 completions of 18 attempts for 79 yd vs 'B' 13 of 30 for 139 yd (PDF 158) — mixture kept defenses honest; 'A' won 7-0. Modern observables that would calibrate it: pre-snap formation/stance features, defender alignment entropy, snap-to-commit reaction dispersion from tracking data. 1922 text itself gives no tracking telemetry: LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE at the individual-reaction level.

primitives.name: Punt territory-exchange policy ('When in doubt, punt' + zone-conditional down rules)
primitives.verbatim_quote: on every perfectly executed punt, backed up by a well drilled team, the ball is given to the opponents in exchange for forty vards of valuable terri- tory
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: x = field position (yards from own goal; length unit yd as printed). d = down number (dimensionless count 1-4). DangerZone/KickArea/ScoringZone = printed zone predicates from the Offensive Strategic Map (printed p. 138 / PDF 152; zones are field-position intervals). Poss = possession boolean. E[Delta y] = expected net field-position exchange per clean punt; 40 yd is the PRINTED approximation ('forty vards', OCR artifact preserved, PDF 151), not a measured modern value. Punt/GiveUpOnDowns = action predicates (dimensionless). Formalization of printed prose rules, no source equation.
primitives.assumptions: Predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rule; the source contains NO equations. Printed rules: '(1) When in doubt, punt. The punt is the strongest offensive as well as defensive play.' '(3) In the danger zone, punt on the first down.' '(5) In the kicking area, punt on the second or third down. Do not wait for the fourth down, because opponents can set themselves for it' '(2) Don't give up the ball on the fourth down, except in the last ten yards or scoring zone.' (all PDF 153, printed p. 139). Assumes a well-drilled coverage team and a perfectly executed punt for the 40-yd exchange; assumes punt superiority is conditional on personnel ('If the quarterback discovers that his team is outclassed in punting, he should punt only when forced to, except when in the danger zone', PDF 153).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The 40-yd exchange collapses when punts are partially blocked: printed 1921 game averages were only ~31 yd ('A', 14 kicks) and ~32 yd ('B', 11 kicks) 'because several kicks were partially blocked' (PDF 159). Fails when outclassed in punting, when the receiver is dangerous (kick out of bounds instead, PDF 153), when wind/time make delay discretion (exception to rule 3, PDF 153), and in the scoring zone where giving up the ball on fourth down is prohibited. The policy is era-bound: 1922 rules (touchback values, fair-catch free-kick option, PDF 173-174) differ from modern rules; do not transplant the zone constants without recalibration.
timescales: tau_0 = pre-snap orientation / signal cadence (order 1-5 s; modeling convention, not printed)
tau_1 = snap-to-first-contact (order 1-3 s; modeling convention)
tau_2 = whole-play execution (order 4-8 s; modeling convention)
tau_3 = drive/game/season learning and system drill (minutes to weeks; modeling convention)

layer2.mapping: Binds to the possession-state transition kernel of the 22-player system: Punt is a controlled transition that flips the Poss boolean while shifting the field-position state x by approximately +40 yd (printed constant), i.e., a deliberate possession sacrifice that buys territory. The zone-conditional down rules are a Markov policy over (x, d): a precompiled decision table the quarterback executes, with the punt as the default action under uncertainty ('when in doubt'). Constraint: no fourth-down turnover outside the scoring zone; the kernel's value is net field position, not possession count.
layer2.telemetry: Printed calibration: 1921 game punt totals 482 yd on 14 kicks vs 351 yd on 11 kicks, averages ~31/~32 yd with partial blocks (PDF 159); tactical error log cites 'A's fourth down punts in Danger Zone causing hurried short punts' (PDF 161). Modern calibration: net punt yardage, hang time, coverage tackle depth, touchback rate. The printed 40-yd figure is an ideal-drill expectation, not a sample mean — treat as prior, update with observed net exchange.

primitives.name: Tertiary information-gated commitment (hold until direction is certain)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The tertiary must play as conservatively as possible and not allow themselves to be drawn from their position until the opponent’s formation or concentration of play has uncoiled itself to such an extent that there is no doubt as to its direction.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: i = defender index in the tertiary (dimensionless). dir = play direction (categorical variable over the field). Certain = predicate matching the printed 'no doubt as to its direction' (truth value, dimensionless). Hold/Advance/Commit = action-state booleans (dimensionless). No physical units: predicate-logic formalization of a printed decision rule, no source equation.
primitives.assumptions: Predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rule; the source contains NO equations. Printed context: the tertiary's 'particular or one duty' is responsibility for everything the primary and secondary cannot handle — 'trick plays, sweeping end runs, forward passes, and onside kicks' (PDF 101). Assumes the play 'uncoils' observable direction over time and that premature commitment is the dominant failure mode ('The tertiary must not run forward too soon or be drawn into the field too far', PDF 101; 'Don't be fooled.', PDF 102). Position prior: slightly outside own end, about eight to eighteen yards back against compact formations (PDF 102).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails if the offense can manufacture false certainty — decoys and crossing routes that make direction appear resolved before it is (Arrangements II and IV, PDF 118, 120: three eligible men run at the tertiary 'causing a fatal hesitation in his play for the ball'). The gate also fails when holding is itself exploited: a safety who never commits lets short completions accumulate; the printed system balances this by assigning short passes to the secondary (PDF 101) so the tertiary's conservatism is bounded by a division of labor. Under double-eligible shifts (PDF 123) direction may never fully resolve pre-snap, so the gate must operate on post-snap evidence only.

tau_1 = snap-to-first-contact (order 1-3 s; modeling convention)
tau_2 = whole-play execution (order 4-8 s; modeling convention)
tau_3 = drive/game/season learning and system drill (minutes to weeks; modeling convention)

layer2.mapping: Binds to the commitment constraint on the defense's transition kernel: each tertiary defender is a controller whose action (Hold vs Commit) is gated by an information predicate on the play-direction posterior. This is an evidence-threshold policy — do not spend the irreversible positional resource (depth/leverage) until the posterior concentrates. In the 22-player system it is the deep-defender analogue of an optimal-stopping rule: the cost of early commitment (being drawn out, 'Don't be fooled') is catastrophic-tail exposure, the cost of waiting is bounded short gains handled by the secondary.
layer2.telemetry: Printed calibration: tertiary depth 8-18 yd vs compact, safety ~18 yd back in pass defense (PDF 137), 20 yd vs compact / 35-50 yd vs open for the safety (PDF 68) — depth is the observable proxy for the conservatism gate. Modern calibration: defender depth-at-snap, commit-time vs ball-release time from tracking, completion rate allowed when deep defenders bite early. Individual belief states: LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE from 1922 text.

primitives.name: Long-pass completion veto (golden rule of pass defense)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The golden rule for the defense is to prevent the comple- tion of all long passes. A completed long pass may mean a touchdown.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: ell = forward-pass event (dimensionless event token); ell_long = long pass subclass (categorical, as printed). PreventComplete/Intercept/KnockDown = defensive action predicates (dimensionless). succ = strict priority ordering (ordinal, dimensionless). BothJump = predicate 'players of both teams are jumping for the ball' (printed). TD_Threat = catastrophic-outcome flag (boolean). No physical units: predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rules, no source equation.
primitives.assumptions: Predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rule; the source contains NO equations. Printed rules: 'It should also be remembered that the defense has as much right to catch the pass as the offense.' 'If players of both teams are jumping for the ball, it is much safer for the defense to knock it down. If opponents are not too near, it is better to try to intercept it, except on the fourth down.' (PDF 20-21). 'The defensive back must start before the offensive player reaches him, so that he may keep between his goal and the receiver. He plays the receiver until he sees the ball and then plays the ball.' (PDF 20). Assumes a touchdown is the dominant loss mode of a completed long pass, and that knock-down is lower-variance than contested interception.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The veto is down-conditional: on fourth down the printed rule flips toward interception (PDF 21) because an incomplete pass ends the drive anyway, so the variance penalty of a contested catch changes sign. Fails when the defender is beaten deep before the gate can act ('A pass caught behind the defensive half may mean a touchdown', PDF 21) — prevention must be positional (start early, stay goal-side), not reactive. Also fails against the printed 'strike the arms of the receiver from behind simultaneously with the catch' tactic (PDF 21) if mistimed: a lunge that misses removes the defender from the play entirely.

tau_2 = whole-play execution (order 4-8 s; modeling convention)
tau_3 = drive/game/season learning and system drill (minutes to weeks; modeling convention)

layer2.mapping: Binds to a tail-risk veto constraint on the defense's action selection: among defensive actions on a pass event, the ordering PreventComplete succ Intercept is a lexicographic risk rule — the catastrophic branch (completed long pass => touchdown) is vetoed before expected-value optimization over interception yards is allowed to run. In the 22-player system this is the deep coverage constraint that dominates greedy ball-hawking; the fourth-down exception is a state-dependent relaxation of the veto when the drive-termination condition changes the payoff structure.
layer2.telemetry: Printed calibration: 1921 game — 'B' completed 6 of 9 first-quarter passes for 56 yd (avg ~6.1 yd), many on third downs; 'A' allowed a 64-yard touchdown march after a double backward pass ending in a forward pass (PDF 160-161) — the catastrophic branch realized. Modern calibration: deep completion rate allowed, air yards per attempt, interception-vs-knockdown contest outcomes by down. Belief/attention states: LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE from the 1922 text.

primitives.name: First-yard control theorem with wedge apex re-election (fault-tolerant point of attack)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The team that controls the first yard beyond the line of scrimmage, all other things being equal, should win.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: y_1 = first yard beyond the line of scrimmage (length unit yd as printed). Control = predicate 'controls the first yard' (truth value). ceteris paribus = printed condition 'all other things being equal'. Win = game-outcome boolean (dimensionless). apex_k = k-th designated wedge leader (player index, dimensionless). Jam = predicate 'forward movement is blocked' (printed). Adhering = set of linemen charging shoulder-to-shoulder toward the apex (dimensionless set). wake = shelter region behind the apex (spatial region, yd-scale). Formalization of printed prose, no source equation.
primitives.assumptions: Predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rule; the source contains NO equations. Printed basis: 'The team that controls the first yard beyond the line of scrimmage, all other things being equal, should win.' (PDF 71, printed p. 57); Zuppke grounds line primacy in 'several years' investigation' with summer-school coaches and ten-week spring-practice experiments (PDF 71). Wedge mechanics: the back runs at a designated lineman, flanks adhere tightly, mass 'either runs the defensive line back, or runs over them, or forces the defense to run out around' (PDF 73). Re-election: 'Should the designated apex run into a jam so that his forward movement is blocked, then one of the adhering linemen immediately becomes a new apex, the supporting linemen squeeze this new apex forward, and the alert back switches from the wake of the first to the wake of the second apex.' (PDF 74).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The ceteris-paribus clause is load-bearing: first-yard control does not win when the secondary is strong and unblocked — the quick-opening method's critics note the secondary arrives at the opening simultaneously with the back, nullifying line blocking (PDF 71-72); Zuppke's fix is a tandem interferer crashing into the first secondary man (PDF 72). Wedge re-election fails if the back cannot read the new apex fast enough ('the alert back switches'), if adhering linemen are not tightly coupled (gaps become alleys, PDF 60), or against a defense that refuses to be compressed and instead spills around the flanks. The claim is a conditional empirical generalization from 1910s-1920s play, not a proved theorem; do not treat 'should win' as a deterministic guarantee.
timescales: tau_0 = pre-snap orientation / signal cadence (order 1-5 s; modeling convention, not printed)
tau_1 = snap-to-first-contact (order 1-3 s; modeling convention)
tau_2 = whole-play execution (order 4-8 s; modeling convention)
tau_3 = drive/game/season learning and system drill (minutes to weeks; modeling convention)

layer2.mapping: Binds to the line-of-scrimmage displacement kernel: the wedge is a distributed, fault-tolerant actuator whose leader (apex) is dynamically re-elected from the adhering set when blocked — a local failover transition that keeps the mass-momentum vector pointed at the defense without central re-planning. State variables: apex index, adhesion coupling, back wake-assignment; constraint: the back must track the current apex, not the original signal. First-yard control is the kernel's success predicate at tau_1; the tandem interferer (PDF 72) extends the kernel's reach into the secondary layer.
layer2.telemetry: Printed calibration: 1921 game rush yards by quarter — 'B' 51/39/65/9 yd vs 'A' 15/24/24/71 (PDF 158, 160): line control fluctuated drive-to-drive and decided the 7-0 result. Modern calibration: yards before contact, line-yardage, stuff rate, first-down conversion on early downs, wedge/mass-play success rate by defensive front. Apex re-election timing: LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE from 1922 text; observable today only via tracking.

primitives.name: Shift two-sided uncertainty tradeoff (disorganize the defense, risk your own assignments)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Therefore, while the shift has a tendency to disorganize the opponent’s line by keep- ing its members guessing as to where to expect its attack, it also has an inherent disorganizing element of uncertainty concerning the exact duties of its own individuals, should they not meet the opponent’s defense lined up as antici- pated.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Shift = pre-snap motion action predicate (dimensionless). D_read = defense's read of the attack (categorical random variable); H = Shannon entropy (bits) — used here as an ordinal uncertainty measure, arrows denote qualitative increase exactly as the printed 'tendency', not a computed value. O_duties = offense's own assignment mapping conditioned on the actual defensive alignment D_actual (categorical random variable; bits). VaryAlign = defense varying its lineup down-to-down (action predicate). Consistency = repeatability of the offense's attack execution (truth value). Formalization of printed prose tradeoff, no source equation; no numerical entropy is claimed.
primitives.assumptions: Predicate-logic formalization of printed prose rule; the source contains NO equations. Printed basis: the shift 'must contain the element of surprise' and 'hinges upon disorganizing the primary line' (PDF 144); its cost is 'an inherent disorganizing element of uncertainty concerning the exact duties of its own individuals' (quoted). Defensive counter printed as an obligation: 'A defense that does not take advantage of that weakness of the shift by varying its own defensive lineup from down to down to break up consistency of the opponent's attack, has failed to make use of one of its greatest assets.' (PDF 144). Seasonal decay: 'As the season advances... neither method has the advantage in games in which the personnel of both teams is of equal ability and under the tutelage of able coaches.' (PDF 145). Rhythm personnel precondition: avoid the shift if men 'lack that sense of rhythm' (PDF 145).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when the defense varies alignment down-to-down (the printed counter), when the offense's own men are cumbersome or rhythm-poor, when drill time for the shift cannibalizes defensive fundamentals ('many defensive details may have to be neglected for lack of time', PDF 145), and late-season against equal, well-coached personnel where the surprise premium decays to zero. Charging signals must not be used in quick shifts (PDF 169) — combining the two destroys the snap-timing advantage. The tradeoff is symmetric: any entropy injected into the defense's read is partially injected into the offense's own assignment map.

The defensive counter (down-to-down alignment variation) is the mirror mixed strategy that breaks the offense's consistency — a minimax-style response in the alignment game. State variables: alignment distributions of both units; constraint: rhythm/drill capacity bounds how much entropy the offense can afford.

reasoning_traces.think: Zuppke's 1922 text is, read against the grain, a treatise on information warfare conducted under extreme time pressure, and the play cycle is its central encoding theorem. The printed completeness rule — one or two straights, one or two slants, one angle, one or two forward passes, all from the same initial formation (PDF 75) — is not a menu of plays; it is a constraint on the offense's observable signature. If every member of the cycle presents the same pre-snap formation, stances, and mannerisms, then the defense's posterior over play types cannot concentrate before the snap. The defense must therefore keep its transition kernel mixed: linemen cannot fully commit to penetration, the secondary cannot fully commit to depth, because either commitment is exploitable by another member of the same cycle. Zuppke makes the mechanism explicit when he writes that the third and fourth plays inherit the mannerisms of the parent first and second, and the forward-pass plays exploit the mannerisms of at least two of the first four (PDF 75). This is deliberate signature reuse: the offense spends its drill budget making distinct actions statistically indistinguishable at the observation boundary, then cashes the defense's hesitation after the snap. The angle play is the sharpest instrument in the cycle because it carries a double threat — the back runs parallel to the scrimmage line with his face toward the sideline until opposite the set opening, then either darts in for a run or steps back for a throw (PDF 75). The run/pass branch point is delayed until the latest possible moment, which maximizes the time the defense's posterior stays unresolved. Note the cost side: Zuppke insists this takes 'an unusual amount of drill' and that neither the forward nor backward move may be telegraphed by looks or actions. Indistinguishability is manufactured, not free. The shift chapter (PDF 144-145) generalizes the same logic into a two-sided entropy budget, and this is where the text is most modern. The shift raises the defense's uncertainty about where the attack will land — it hopes to catch each lineman 'off balance and, so to speak, each on one foot' — but Zuppke immediately prices the cost: the offense itself cannot know whether its opponents will be lined up slightly left, directly in front, slightly right, or with six or seven men on the primary line, so the shift carries 'an inherent disorganizing element of uncertainty concerning the exact duties of its own individuals.' Entropy injected into the opponent's read is partially injected into your own assignment map. The net advantage is a difference of two uncertainties, bounded by personnel rhythm and drill time. And the defensive counter is printed as an obligation: vary the defensive lineup from down to down to break the consistency of the shift's attack. That is a mixed-strategy response in the alignment game — the defense refuses to be a stationary distribution the shift can exploit. Zuppke even prints the decay law: the shift runs up larger scores against ordinary opponents and bothers anyone early in the season, but as the season advances neither method has the advantage between equal, well-coached teams. The surprise premium is a transient, arbitraged away by film study and repetition. The commitment gates on defense close the loop. The tertiary must hold position until the play has 'uncoiled itself' so there is 'no doubt as to its direction' (PDF 101), and the safety must not leave position unless certain he can execute his intentions (PDF 68). These are evidence-threshold policies: do not spend the irreversible positional resource until the posterior concentrates. The offense's entire cycle-and-shift apparatus exists to manufacture false certainty — decoys that draw the tertiary (PDF 117), three eligible men running at him to cause 'a fatal hesitation' (PDF 118), crossing paths (PDF 120). The defense's answer is division of labor: the secondary owns short passes so the tertiary can afford to wait (PDF 101), and the golden rule vetoes the catastrophic branch — prevent completion of all long passes, because a completed long pass may mean a touchdown (PDF 20). Read together, these rules form a coherent minimax architecture: encode indistinguishably, gate commitment on evidence, and lexicographically veto the tail before optimizing the mean.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The hidden state behind Zuppke's information rules is a sequence of historical scars. The forward pass itself was a rules-committee intervention: 'When the rules committee added the forward pass, they built up the game with a new series of constructive fundamentals' (PDF 114), and the screened pass existed as far back as 1906 precisely because coaches were ignorant of how much blocking the linemen ought to do to protect the thrower — 'Many passes were intercepted and carried back for a touchdown' (PDF 121). Oak Park High School's 1910-1912 teams then ran the screen almost entirely, often from a double pass with one lateral (PDF 121). The protection-first screen doctrine is thus scar tissue from interception returns, not abstract design. The shift lineage is equally concrete: the Minnesota-style tackles-back shift, the Chicago-style U formation, Illinois' own three-part shift, and Iowa's one-hep guards-back shift from its 1921 Western Conference championship drive (PDF 146-148). Zuppke's summer school — twenty-two lectures, nine years, about twelve hundred coaches from up to thirty-seven states in a single year (PDF 9) — is the diffusion network that turned these local mutations into shared doctrine, and his ten-week spring-practice experiments (PDF 71) are the selection mechanism. The 1921 Big Ten game charted in Chapter XII, won 7-0 by 'A' after a double backward pass ending in a forward pass destroyed 'B's defensive morale for a 64-yard march (PDF 161), is the empirical wound that validates the whole deception architecture.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The text is a recursive belief engine. The quarterback must mask intentions because 'the eyes of the defense are studying him' (PDF 67); the secondary watches the quarterback's eyes and body for tells, and the backs' stances and the designated receiver's excitement-induced tightening (PDF 100). So the offense models the defense modeling it: the secondary is coached to move about a little so the offensive interferers 'cannot know where to expect to find their men' (PDF 100), and if the opponent's quarterback is studying the secondary, the secondary should mislead him about its intended position at the snap (PDF 101). The tertiary's gate is third-order: he must not be drawn by what the offense wants him to believe ('Don't be fooled', PDF 102), while the offense's decoys exist to manufacture exactly that false belief. Under pressure the clash is concrete: the coach's comfort call (a conservative waiting end) versus the defensive coordinator's tendency trap (a plunging end paired with a conservative tackle so the space between them never becomes an alley, PDF 59-60) versus the quarterback's internal clock — the general who must respect the system's law of averages yet retain enough flexibility to extricate it from a groove (PDF 150). The 'man across' yell (PDF 137) is an explicit belief-update protocol between defenders when a receiver crosses zones.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Physics and psychology veto high-EV calls at several printed joints. The lunge veto: a lineman who lunges away from his base and misses is out of the play (PDF 42), so the mechanically explosive first step is vetoed by balance conservation — run into the opponent, do not lunge. The attention veto: the four-threat man (run, throw, punt, drop kick) taxes the defense's sustained attention and morale until individuals act 'like a leaderless mob' (PDF 114), but the same overload on one's own quarterback — directing, carrying, punting, throwing, blocking, receiving, tackling — creates 'exhaustion, injury, or overheated brain' precisely when best judgment is needed (PDF 66), so the system vetoes loading the general. The tail veto: a completed long pass may mean a touchdown (PDF 20), which lexicographically dominates any interception-yardage gain, except on fourth down where drive termination flips the calculus (PDF 21). And the complexity veto: overloading the team with plays 'will cause indecision on the part of the general and the players, and develop a flabby attack' (PDF 74) — cognitive bandwidth is a hard constraint that vetoes theoretically richer schemes.

reasoning_traces.think: The second sovereign thread in Zuppke is territorial economics under uncertainty, and its kernel is the punt. The printed exchange invariant — on every perfectly executed punt, backed up by a well-drilled team, the ball is given to the opponents in exchange for forty yards of valuable territory (PDF 151, OCR 'vards' preserved) — reframes possession from an asset to be hoarded into a currency to be spent at a favorable rate. The zone-conditional policy that implements it is a precompiled Markov decision table: in the danger zone punt on first down; in the kicking area punt on second or third, never wait for fourth because opponents can set themselves for it; do not give up the ball on fourth down except in the last ten yards or scoring zone; when in doubt, punt (PDF 153). Every rule is a field-position-dependent action prior, and the system exists to stop the quarterback from improvising against it. The printed 1921 game is the calibration set and the cautionary tale at once: punt averages of roughly 31 and 32 yards, short 'because several kicks were partially blocked' (PDF 159), and the tactical error log explicitly condemns 'A's fourth down punts in the Danger Zone causing hurried short punts' (PDF 161). The ideal forty-yard exchange is a drill-condition expectation; the realized exchange is a random variable degraded by block probability, wind, and receiver quality. Zuppke's own exceptions encode the degradation: outclassed in punting, punt only when forced except in the danger zone; against a dangerous receiver kick out of bounds; against an erratic receiver kick high so the ends can hunt fumbles (PDF 153). The policy is therefore not dogma but a prior with printed update rules. The first-yard control theorem supplies the micro-foundation: the team that controls the first yard beyond the line of scrimmage, all other things being equal, should win (PDF 71). Zuppke ranks the line above the backs because the attack hinges on it to a greater degree, and he grounds the claim in years of investigation with summer-school coaches and spring-practice experiments rather than assertion. The two line methods — quick openings for the back to dart through, versus the adhesive wedge that forces the defense to run out around — are alternative kernels for producing that first yard, and Zuppke declares both of equal merit. The wedge's fault tolerance is the remarkable part: when the designated apex jams, an adhering lineman immediately becomes the new apex, the supporting linemen squeeze him forward, and the alert back switches wakes (PDF 74). This is distributed failover without central replanning — the point of attack is a property of the mass, not of one designated body. The quick-opening method's weakness is printed too: a strong secondary arrives at the opening simultaneously with the back and nullifies the line's blocking, so Zuppke adds the tandem interferer who crashes into the first secondary man just as he comes up to tackle (PDF 72). Each kernel carries its own counter and its own patch. Finally, the generalship chapter binds the economics to the agent: the coaches must compel the quarterback to respect the law of averages and discriminate sound football from the go-as-you-please hit-or-miss kind (PDF 149-150); he must realize that trying to be superior to the system makes him a disorganizer apt to guide his team to defeat; yet the system must stay flexible enough to let him use native shrewdness (PDF 150). This is a bounded-authority executor: a compiled policy with a deviation budget, where the deviation budget is itself conditioned on score and clock — receive the kick-off only when seven points behind with about five minutes left (PDF 153), no dangerous plays in the kicking area unless behind with ten minutes left (PDF 156). The territorial kernel, the first-yard kernel, and the bounded-executor constraint compose into a single decision architecture: spend possession for territory at the printed rate, win the first yard with fault-tolerant mass, and let the agent deviate only where the game state has re-priced risk.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The territorial doctrine descends from the mass-momentum era and its discontents. The wedge is the fossil of 1890s mass play, re-engineered by Zuppke into an adhesive, re-electing apex rather than a fixed flying wedge; the quick-opening method is the older alternative he explicitly names 'the first and older of the two methods' (PDF 71). His evidence base is institutional: nine years of a summer coaching school reaching about twelve hundred coaches (PDF 9), ten-week spring-practice sessions used as experiments (PDF 71), and the charted 1921 Big Ten game — a 7-0 result in which 'B' out-gained 'A' 394 to 256 total yards yet lost, because 'A' converted a double-backward-pass deception into a 64-yard touchdown march and played conservative kicking-area football for three quarters (PDF 159, 161). That game is the scar that teaches yardage totals do not decide games; field position at decisive moments and morale collapse do. The strategic map (PDF 152) and the quarterback/captain suggestion lists (PDF 153-157) are the compiled lessons of those games, and the captain's rules — elect to kick off, take risks only to stop excessive gains, take out time when opponents gain consistently but never when going good (PDF 155-157) — encode clock-and-score state dependence learned from played history.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The generalship chapter is an explicit principal-agent model. The spectator believes the quarterback does all the thinking; Zuppke corrects this: the quarterback is guided by the system, and all the men plus the coaches are part of that system (PDF 149). The coach is the principal who compiles years of game history into formations and play cycles that 'implant themselves firmly in his memory', and the quarterback is the agent whose on-field belief state must stay aligned with that compilation. The failure mode is named: as soon as he tries to be superior to the system he proves himself a disorganizer (PDF 150). Yet the principal must not over-constrain: the system must be flexible enough to allow native shrewdness, must not obscure the individual entirely, and must deal with human nature, 'a variable quantity which often refuses to stay put' (PDF 150). Under pressure the clash is three-way: the coach's compiled conservatism (punt when in doubt), the captain's risk oversight (no dangerous kicking-area plays unless behind with ten minutes left, PDF 156), and the quarterback's live read of which plays are actually working against this particular opponent — 'not preconceived as successful plays, but the plays that are actually working' (PDF 154). The defense reads the same agent: the secondary watches the quarterback's eyes for tells (PDF 100), so the agent must mask even his belief updates.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The territorial kernel is vetoed by physics and physiology at printed boundaries. Wind and field condition veto the ideal exchange: the punter must kick high with the wind, low against it, long and low for out of bounds (PDF 24), and on slippery fields the stance must keep weight over the left foot to reduce slipping (PDF 22) — the forty-yard prior is conditioned on traction and air. The block-probability veto: any punting method that consumes time or covers too much ground raises the probability of a blocked punt (PDF 23-24), which is why the one-step and one-and-a-half-step kicks are preferred and why the three-wave punt protection exists (PDF 105). The fatigue veto on the agent: loading the quarterback with every duty creates exhaustion, injury, or overheated brain just when best judgment is needed (PDF 66), so the system relieves him of physical dexterity tasks to protect the decision organ. And the tail veto sits over everything: a completed long pass may mean a touchdown (PDF 20), so no amount of expected territorial gain justifies leaving the deep branch unvetoed; the captain's rule to take risks only to stop excessive gains (PDF 157) is the same lexicographic priority expressed as game management.

universal_lens: Polymath audit lens: Zuppke 1922 is a pre-formal theory of adversarial information design and bounded rationality — encoder indistinguishability (play cycles), two-sided entropy budgets (the shift), evidence-gated optimal stopping (tertiary commitment), lexicographic tail vetoes (long-pass golden rule), and fault-tolerant distributed control (wedge apex re-election). Audit any modern decision system by asking whether its observable signatures leak, whether its uncertainty injections price their own cost, and whether its catastrophic branches are vetoed before expected-value optimization runs.
gsi_mapping: GSI binding: the commitment gates and attention-overload rules map to clinical decision telemetry under time pressure — the tertiary's hold-until-certain is an evidence-threshold diagnostic rule, and the quarterback overload scar (exhaustion, injury, overheated brain impairing judgment at the critical moment, PDF 66) is a cognitive-fatigue patient-safety constraint. The tackling mechanics (head to one side, arms below shoulders, shoulder-to-thigh with leg drive, PDF 33-35) are axonal-shear-relevant impact geometry: the printed instruction to keep the head to one side to avoid injury (PDF 33) and the warning that a head caught on the thighs invites roll-over injury (PDF 35) are early concussion-mechanics doctrine. Bioenergetic load management appears as the coach's relief of the general from physical duties to preserve decision capacity. All mappings are structural analogies, not clinical measurements; the 1922 text supplies no physiological telemetry.
gse_mapping: GSE binding: the play cycle is a deception encoder for the Coach-Mind sim — hold the pre-snap observation channel constant across a run/pass mixture so the simulated defense posterior stays mixed; the shift tradeoff calibrates how much pre-snap motion entropy a personnel group can afford before its own assignment map degrades. The punt policy is a field-position value kernel for drive simulation and DFS/portfolio tail management: possession is currency spent at a printed ~40-yd rate, degraded by block probability (1921 realized averages ~31-32 yd), and the long-pass golden rule is the lexicographic veto that forbids optimizing mean outcomes while the touchdown branch is open. The bounded-executor generalship model (compiled system plus score/clock-conditioned deviation budget) is the architecture for any autonomous play-calling agent. Internal research only; no odds inputs, no publication.
